## How to work

Read the preparation material first, then work in groups of three or four. The reading takes **15 minutes** and the tasks **75 minutes** — one 90-minute class. Choose a discussion lead, a note-taker and a spokesperson, and rotate the roles between tasks. Open each self-check answer only after you have written down your own reasoning.

**All persons, events and circumstances are fictional**; the cases are adapted from the course case banks. For every case answer the same four questions: **Does the patient have decision-making capacity, and how do you know? Who decides, and under which article? Is this Art. 89(2), Art. 90(4) or neither? What will you do now, and what will you document?** You are assessed on the correct Bulgarian legal basis and on a decision in which the patient is informed, involved and not abandoned.

## Task 1. The obliging nurse — 10 minutes

A surgeon phones the ward nurse and asks her to "get the written consent" for tomorrow's operation. The patient signs without reading. After surgery a wound infection develops — a complication listed in the form but never explained by the physician. The patient complains that he was not informed. Is the complaint well-founded? What was the nurse's correct role? What does the signature prove?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer: the duty to inform is the physician's"}

The complaint about information is **well-founded**. The duty to inform lies with the treating physician (Health Act, Art. 88(1)), and for surgery both the information and the consent are written (Art. 89(1)). The nurse may support the process — deliver the form, answer practical questions, tell the doctor that the patient has questions — but cannot replace the physician's explanation, and should refuse to "collect a signature" alone.

A signature shows that a form was signed, not that the patient was informed. The infection itself is not proof of fault: a known complication of correctly performed surgery does not establish negligence. The problem is the missing explanation. A complaint can go to the Regional Health Inspectorate (Art. 93) and, for an ethics breach, to the BMA regional college.

:::

## Task 2. Counselling at sixteen — 15 minutes

A 16-year-old girl comes alone for a preventive gynaecological examination and contraceptive counselling. At the end she asks whether an intrauterine device can be inserted today and whether her parents "will find out". She is healthy; there is no emergency. What may the physician do without a parent? Do the counselling and the IUD follow the same rule? What can be promised about confidentiality?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer: counselling yes, IUD with a parent"}

Counselling on sexual and reproductive health, a preventive examination and a pregnancy test need **no parental consent from age 16** (Health Act, Art. 87(3); Ordinance No. 8/2018, Arts 2–4). Inserting an IUD is a medical intervention outside the Ordinance, so it needs **her consent and a parent's** (Art. 87(2)).

If a disease or abnormality is found, the physician must notify the parent (Ordinance, Art. 5), so the limits of confidentiality are explained at the outset — absolute secrecy is not promised. Offer support for talking to a parent, give accurate information about methods (including condoms against infections), and check tactfully that the relationship is voluntary and free of exploitation (Child Protection Act, Art. 7).

:::

## Task 3. Art. 89(2) or Art. 90(4)? — 15 minutes

Distinguish Health Act Art. 89(2) from Art. 90(4). Then classify: (a) a 10-year-old with a severed artery whose parents cannot be reached; (b) parents who refuse a transfusion for their seriously anaemic 10-year-old; (c) a 68-year-old who refuses surgery for internal bleeding after a suicide attempt.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer: consent cannot be obtained vs consent refused"}

Under **Art. 89(2)**, life is immediately threatened and the patient cannot express consent (and a required representative cannot be reached in time); the team acts in the patient's health interest without written consent. Under **Art. 90(4)**, the patient or representative **has refused** and life is threatened; the **head of the medical establishment** may decide on life-saving treatment — a discretionary decision of a designated person, not an automatic power of every clinician.

(a) **Art. 89(2)**, with the Blood Act, Art. 32: surgery and transfusion proceed; keep trying to reach the parents and document the threat, the attempts and who decided. The teacher's signature has no legal value.
(b) **Art. 90(4)**: the parents' refusal is documented; the head may decide on life-saving treatment; the Blood Act (Arts 31–33) also applies, and a child at risk triggers notification of the Social Assistance Directorate. Parents may refuse for themselves what they may not refuse for their child.
(c) **Art. 90(4)** — after a rapid, documented capacity assessment. Suicidal intent raises concern about capacity but does not by itself establish incapacity; losing consciousness does not cancel the refusal; psychiatric measures (Arts 153–155) alone do not authorise surgery.

:::

## Task 4. A finding under anaesthesia — 15 minutes

During a polypectomy under general anaesthesia, frozen section shows an early cancer of the nasal turbinate. Removing the turbinate now would spare a second anaesthetic; the patient's wife is in the waiting room. May the surgeon remove the turbinate now? Can the wife consent? How could the dilemma have been prevented?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer: finish the polypectomy, inform, obtain new consent"}

**No.** Consent covered the polypectomy only, and an early cancer is not an immediate threat to life, so Art. 89(2) does not apply; staging and treatment planning can safely wait. The **wife cannot consent** for an adult who will regain capacity within hours — a spouse is not among the persons listed in Art. 87, and "relatives" in Code Art. 26 creates no representative authority.

The surgeon completes the polypectomy, informs the patient and obtains new written consent. Sparing a second anaesthetic is a real benefit, but it is the patient's trade-off to make. Prevention: discuss foreseeable findings before surgery and record what the patient authorises ("if a tumour is found, I agree / do not agree to …").

:::

## Task 5. Who should decide? — 15 minutes

An unconscious 45-year-old after a car crash needs either amputation (higher survival, loss of the limb) or a complex reconstruction (higher risk of death, chance to keep the leg); delay of more than a few hours increases the risk. His parents want amputation; his wife wants "everything possible to save the leg". Who decides, what weight do the relatives' views have, and how is the decision documented?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer: no legal representative; the team decides in his interest"}

An adult without interdiction has **no legal representative**, so neither the wife nor the parents consent for him (Art. 87). If life is immediately threatened and he cannot consent, the team decides in his health interest (Art. 89(2)); if there is time, the irreversible choice is delayed. His **previously expressed wishes** must be taken into account (Oviedo, Art. 9).

The relatives are heard as **witnesses of his values** — work, sport, attitude to disability and risk — not as decision-makers. A consultation among physicians (consilium, Code Art. 38) supports the judgement but creates no consent authority. Be transparent with both sides of the family and document the reasons, the information gathered about his wishes and who took part.

:::

## Individual final task — 5 minutes

Answer briefly without opening the answers:

1. Name the five elements of valid consent.
2. A 17-year-old asks for a circumcision without his parents' knowledge. What does the law require, and what options can the urologist offer?
3. An 84-year-old with mild cognitive decline refuses an amputation. Name the four abilities you would assess.

### Feedback criteria

A complete answer treats consent as a process with five elements; places the duty to inform on the treating physician (Art. 88) and the written form where Art. 89(1) requires it; separates legal capacity (a status) from decision-making capacity (a clinical judgement for one decision); applies Art. 87 and Ordinance No. 8/2018 correctly to minors; keeps Art. 89(2) and Art. 90(4) apart; and documents the decision. Treating relatives of an adult as legal representatives, or a refusal as proof of incapacity, does not complete the task.
